messages.subject: OperandsAndPartials clarification and speedups
parts:
On 6/3/13 3:09 PM, Peter Li wrote:

> When we use OperandsAndPartials, doesn't it return a var (as opposed to a double)?

I see why you may think that given the name "to_var", but it
depends on the instantiation of the return type. If the
return type is double, then all of the arrays of vari will
be empty and you'll just get the return value.

I did have some comments on the current form of the class.

1. There's a static boolean defined in the class that's not
used anywhere else in src/stan:

const static bool all_constant = is_constant<T_return_type>::value;

2. The current implementation imposes a high construction overhead
due to all of the calls to length() and addition (15 total multiplies,
15 total adds). Since we're guaranteed order on initialization, can't
each take the pointer produced by the last to cut down the O(n^2)
to O(n)? So this:

d_x1(all_partials),
d_x2(all_partials
+ (!is_constant_struct<T1>::value) * length(x1)),
d_x3(all_partials
+ (!is_constant_struct<T1>::value) * length(x1)
+ (!is_constant_struct<T2>::value) * length(x2)),

would become something with 5 adds and 5 multiplies:

d_x1(all_partials),
d_x2(d_x1.ptr() + (is_constant_struct<T1>::value * length(x1)),
d_x3(d_x2.ptr() + (is_constant_struct<T2>::value * length(x2)),
...
d_x6...

I really wish the ternary op short-circuited! Given that it doesnt, it
might be better to put this in the operation block, especially given that
none of it is defined as const.

{
d_x1.ptr() = all_partials;
if (is_constant_struct<T1>::value)
d_x2.ptr() = d_x1.ptr()
else
d_x2.ptr() = d_x1.ptr() + length(x1);
...
}

Then there are no multiplies and only as many adds as non-constant
arguments.

On the subject of optimization, I have a silly question.
I just used arrays everywhere because I find it easier
to understand, but would it behoove us to change things
like this:

inline size_t set(agrad::vari** varis, const T& x) {
for (size_t n = 0; n < length(x); n++)
varis[n] = x[n].vi_;
return length(x);
}

to pointer arithmetic:

for (...) {
*varis = *x.vi_;
++varis;
++x;
}

or does it matter if you change the above to postifx ++?

*varis++ = (*x++).vi_;

and if so, would this be best:

if (length(x) > 0)
*varis = *x.vi_;
for (size_t n = 1; n < length(x); ++n)
*++varis = (*++x).vi_;

or would the extra conditional unfolding be a killer (no
more conditional evals, but I can see it being less prone
to inline, harder to branch predict, etc.)?

I can make the changes in the form of a pull request,
but I know Daniel's in the middle of an expansion and I
didn't want to create conflicts.

- Bob

P.S. I don't know why this bugs me so much, but while you're at it,
could you make these consistent:

struct set_varis <T,true,false>{

struct set_varis<agrad::var, false, false> {

I prefer the second, or even the second minus the spaces after the
commas. Though I add space if the argument's really huge.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] OperandsAndPartials clarification and speedups
parts:
On 6/4/13 11:12 AM, Peter Li wrote:
> Ah, but in order to use OperandsAndPartials with the cdf, don't I need to take in the typename bool propto?

You can just set propto=false to get the current behavior.

A more general solution would be to add propto template
parameters to the CDFs. That would then let us generate
code for CDFs from truncation and censoring that included
propto=true and perhaps save a lot of calculation.

Eventually, propto may come into play when we roll the
CDFs into the probability functions for truncation and
censoring. As Michael pointed out when he wrote the
CDFs, that would allow us to reuse more subexpressions.
I think there's a truncated normal in there now, but
I'm not sure how efficient it is.

- Bob

I think I understand what you're saying, but for some reason
OperandsAndPartials is doing something weird. I have the following code

for (size_t n = 0; n < N; n++) {
const double y_dbl = value_of(y_vec[n]);
const double y_sqr = y_dbl * y_dbl;
const double inv_sigma_sqr = inv_sigma[n] * inv_sigma[n];
const double exp_val = exp(-0.5 * y_sqr * inv_sigma_sqr);
if (include_summand<false,T_y,T_scale>::value)
cdf *= (1.0 - exp_val);

//gradients
const double exp_div_1m_exp = exp_val / (1.0 - exp_val);
if (!is_constant_struct<T_y>::value)
operands_and_partials.d_x1[n] += y_dbl * inv_sigma_sqr
* exp_div_1m_exp;
if (!is_constant_struct<T_scale>::value)
operands_and_partials.d_x2[n] -= y_sqr * inv_sigma_sqr
* inv_sigma[n] * exp_div_1m_exp;
}

for (size_t n = 0; n < N; n++) {
operands_and_partials.d_x1[n] *= cdf;
operands_and_partials.d_x2[n] *= cdf;
}

return operands_and_partials.to_var(cdf);

But, all of the operands_and_partials.d_x1[n] are off by a factor of one
cdf. In the last for loop (where I multiply by cdf), the
operands_and_partials.d_x1[n] are multiplied by cdf twice, not once. I
think this has to do with the way operands_and_partials is set up, but I
haven't been able to make sense of all of OperandsAndPartials yet.

I think something of the nature of

for (size_t n = 0; n < N; n++) {
const double y_dbl = value_of(y_vec[n]);
const double y_sqr = y_dbl * y_dbl;
const double inv_sigma_sqr = inv_sigma[n] * inv_sigma[n];
const double exp_val = exp(-0.5 * y_sqr * inv_sigma_sqr);
if (include_summand<false,T_y,T_scale>::value)
cdf *= (1.0 - exp_val);
}

for (size_t n = 0; n < N; n++) {
const double y_dbl = value_of(y_vec[n]);
const double y_sqr = y_dbl * y_dbl;
const double inv_sigma_sqr = inv_sigma[n] * inv_sigma[n];
const double exp_val = exp(-0.5 * y_sqr * inv_sigma_sqr);

//gradients
const double exp_div_1m_exp = exp_val / (1.0 - exp_val);
if (!is_constant_struct<T_y>::value)
operands_and_partials.d_x1[n] += y_dbl * inv_sigma_sqr
* exp_div_1m_exp * cdf;
if (!is_constant_struct<T_scale>::value)
operands_and_partials.d_x2[n] -= y_sqr * inv_sigma_sqr
* inv_sigma[n] * exp_div_1m_exp * cdf;
}

should work, but I'm not sure if this is the most efficient.

Peter
